library(knitr)

# Glossary {#sec-glossary .unnumbered}

A reference of statistics and data-science terms used throughout the book. Terms are listed alphabetically. Where a topic is treated in more depth in a chapter, a link is provided.

---

## Aesthetic mapping {#sec-gloss-aes .unnumbered}

The link between a variable in your data and a visual property of a plot — for example, mapping the `wind_speed` variable to the *x*-axis position. Specified inside the `aes()` function in `ggplot2`. Distinct from a *setting*, where a visual property is fixed without reference to data (e.g., `geom_point(alpha = 0.2)`). See @sec-grammarofgraphics.

## Alternative hypothesis {#sec-gloss-alt-hypothesis .unnumbered}

Written $H_a$ or $H_1$. The claim a hypothesis test is gathering evidence *for* — typically that an effect, difference, or relationship exists. Always paired with a null hypothesis ($H_0$). See @sec-hypothesis-testing.

## Bootstrap distribution {#sec-gloss-bootstrap .unnumbered}

The distribution of a statistic computed from many resamples (with replacement) of a single observed sample. Used to construct confidence intervals without theoretical formulas. See @sec-confidence-intervals.

## Categorical variable {#sec-gloss-categorical .unnumbered}

A variable whose values fall into discrete groups or categories — e.g., `carrier`, `origin`, `condition`. Contrast with a *quantitative variable*. See @sec-getting-started.

## Confidence interval {#sec-gloss-ci .unnumbered}

A range of plausible values for an unknown population parameter, constructed from sample data. A 95% confidence interval is built so that, in the long run, 95% of intervals constructed this way would contain the true parameter. See @sec-confidence-intervals.

## Data frame {#sec-gloss-data-frame .unnumbered}

The standard rectangular data structure in R: rows are observations, columns are variables. ModernDive uses the `tibble` flavor of data frames provided by the tidyverse.

## dplyr verb {#sec-gloss-dplyr-verb .unnumbered}

One of the data-transformation functions in the `dplyr` package: `filter()`, `select()`, `mutate()`, `arrange()`, `summarize()`, `group_by()`, and the `*_join()` family. Each verb takes a data frame and returns a transformed data frame. See @sec-wrangling.

## Geometric object (geom) {#sec-gloss-geom .unnumbered}

The visual mark used to represent data in a `ggplot2` plot — `geom_point()` for points, `geom_line()` for lines, `geom_bar()` for bars, etc. The third component of the grammar of graphics. See @sec-grammarofgraphics.

## Grammar of graphics {#sec-gloss-grammar .unnumbered}

A theoretical framework that builds plots from layered components: data, aesthetic mappings, geometric objects, and (optionally) facets, scales, and coordinate systems. Implemented in R by the `ggplot2` package. See @sec-grammarofgraphics.

## Hypothesis test {#sec-gloss-hypothesis-test .unnumbered}

A formal procedure for using sample data to evaluate competing claims (the null hypothesis vs. an alternative hypothesis) about a population. Typically yields a *p*-value used to decide whether to reject $H_0$. See @sec-hypothesis-testing.

## LINE conditions {#sec-gloss-line .unnumbered}

The four assumptions for inference on a regression model: **L**inearity of the relationship, **I**ndependence of observations, **N**ormality of residuals, and **E**quality (homoscedasticity) of residual variance. Diagnostic plots are used to assess each. See @sec-inference-for-regression.

## Linear regression {#sec-gloss-lm .unnumbered}

A model expressing a numerical outcome variable as a linear combination of one or more predictor variables, fit by minimizing the sum of squared residuals. Implemented in R by `lm()`. See @sec-regression.

## Null distribution {#sec-gloss-null-dist .unnumbered}

The sampling distribution of a test statistic *under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true*. Permutation tests construct it empirically by repeatedly shuffling the data. See @sec-hypothesis-testing.

## Null hypothesis {#sec-gloss-null-hypothesis .unnumbered}

Written $H_0$. The claim of "no effect, no difference, no relationship" that a hypothesis test attempts to reject. The starting assumption against which evidence is weighed. See @sec-hypothesis-testing.

## p-value {#sec-gloss-p-value .unnumbered}

The probability — *assuming the null hypothesis is true* — of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained from the sample. Small p-values are evidence against $H_0$. **Not** the probability that $H_0$ is true. See @sec-hypothesis-testing.

## Permutation test {#sec-gloss-permutation .unnumbered}

A simulation-based hypothesis test that constructs the null distribution by repeatedly shuffling labels in the data, breaking any real association. See @sec-hypothesis-testing.

## Pipe operator (`|>`) {#sec-gloss-pipe .unnumbered}

The base-R forward pipe: `x |> f()` is equivalent to `f(x)`. Used to chain a sequence of transformations into a readable left-to-right pipeline. See @sec-piping.

## Point estimate {#sec-gloss-point-estimate .unnumbered}

A single-number guess at an unknown population parameter, computed from sample data — e.g., the sample mean $\bar{x}$ as an estimate of the population mean $\mu$. Contrast with an *interval estimate* (confidence interval). See @sec-confidence-intervals.

## Population parameter {#sec-gloss-population-param .unnumbered}

A numerical summary of an entire population (e.g., the true mean weight $\mu$ of all almonds in a bowl). Usually unknown; the goal of inference is to estimate it from sample data. Contrast with a *sample statistic*. See @sec-sampling.

## Quantitative variable {#sec-gloss-quantitative .unnumbered}

A variable whose values are numerical and meaningful to do arithmetic with — e.g., `wind_speed`, `dep_delay`, `price`. Contrast with a *categorical variable*. See @sec-getting-started.

## Residual {#sec-gloss-residual .unnumbered}

The vertical distance between an observed data point and the value predicted by a regression model: $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$. Residuals being small (in aggregate) means the model fits well. See @sec-regression.

## Sample statistic {#sec-gloss-sample-statistic .unnumbered}

A numerical summary computed from a sample, used to estimate a population parameter (e.g., $\bar{x}$ estimating $\mu$, $\hat{p}$ estimating $p$). Sample statistics vary from sample to sample — that variability is what *sampling distributions* describe. See @sec-sampling.

## Sampling distribution {#sec-gloss-sampling-dist .unnumbered}

The distribution of a sample statistic across all possible samples of a given size from the same population. The key concept underlying all of statistical inference: it tells you how much your point estimate would vary if you took a different sample. See @sec-sampling.

## Standard error {#sec-gloss-se .unnumbered}

The standard deviation of a sampling distribution; quantifies how much a sample statistic typically varies from sample to sample. Smaller standard error = more precise estimates. See @sec-sampling.

## Tidy data {#sec-gloss-tidy .unnumbered}

A standard data layout: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each type of observational unit is its own table. Tidy data is the input format expected by the tidyverse packages. See @sec-tidy-data-ex.

## Tidyverse {#sec-gloss-tidyverse .unnumbered}

A collection of R packages designed with a shared philosophy and consistent interface for data science: `ggplot2`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`, `readr`, `purrr`, `tibble`, `stringr`, and `forcats`. Loaded together via `library(tidyverse)`. See @sec-tidyverse-package.

## Type I error {#sec-gloss-type-i .unnumbered}

Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true — a "false positive." The probability of a Type I error is set by the significance level $\alpha$ (commonly 0.05). See @sec-hypothesis-testing.

## Type II error {#sec-gloss-type-ii .unnumbered}

Failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false — a "false negative." The probability is denoted $\beta$; statistical *power* is $1 - \beta$. See @sec-hypothesis-testing.
